A bit curious about your edit...specifically this part:

Communication, rail and air travel?

In regards to...? Rail is a bit different, as where roads are typically laid only by municipalities, rail can be laid by either governments or private interests. It's more like a pipeline than a interstate highway system.

As for air travel, government has a vested interest in regulating air travel, only one reason being national security. If the government doesn't have knowledge of what aircraft are in the air, and where, then it would be trivial for a foreign power, say China or Russia, to invade national airspace with aircraft of their own...aircraft whose intentions might not be so benevolent as passenger air travel.

As for communications, afaiaao, cell towers and analog lines have been laid by private corporations instead of governments for at least the past 20 years, now. So how would they be subsidized?
My edit was really just a question about all the categories in general. Can they be considered subsidized at all, to what extent, that whole deal.

Passenger Rail, I don't really think can be. The closest thing to that in the US is Amtrak, which is government-owned, in the first place. As far as Industrial Rail goes, most of those rails, to my knowledge, were laid by private companies, not government infrastructure projects. So it's at least not subsidized the same way the interstate highway system is, if it is, at all.

As for Passenger Air, the government has a vested interest in regulating air travel, as I mentioned earlier. I suppose whether or not one considers this to be a 'subsidy' would depend on who you ask...but I am under the impression the Airline companies would prefer to be out from under the various regulations of the FAA, so I would call it less a subsidy, and more a regulatory burden, on the Airlines.

As for communications, perhaps back during the time when governments still laid copper line for analog, and when Southwestern Bell was a monolithical public utility...but as I mentioned, in more recent times, most line and cell towers are placed by private companies, so the infrastructure isn't subsidized today the way the interstate highway system is, if it is at all. If you have some other hypothesis as to how they may be subsidized, I'd be glad to consider it.
